intro: Everything here is free to use in your classroom. Each plant has a printable fact sheet, the games work on any phone or Chromebook, and nothing needs a login.

lessons.title: The great canoe debate
lessons.text: Students play Pack the canoe alone first and write down their eight plants. Then put them in crews of four. Each crew has to agree on one shared list of eight and defend it to the class. Expect real arguments about whether rope matters more than medicine. Finish by reading the "What the voyagers actually did" reveal together.
questions: Which plant was the hardest to leave behind? What would your crew have lost without it?
The voyagers brought plants for ceremony as well as for food. Why might that have mattered as much as eating?
What would you pack today if you were settling a new place and could never go back for more?

lessons.title: Plan a canoe plant garden
lessons.time: Two or three class periods, or a long term project
lessons.text: Using the Grow it notes on the plant pages, students design a small school garden with three canoe plants. They have to match each plant to the sun and water your campus really has, draw a planting plan, and make a calendar that shows when each plant could be harvested. Kī, ʻuala, and kō are forgiving first choices in most parts of Hawaiʻi.
questions: Is your campus more like the wet windward side or the dry leeward side? Which canoe plants fit?
Most canoe plants are grown from cuttings, not seeds. What are the good and bad sides of that for a farmer?
Who on campus or in your community already grows one of these plants and could teach you?

lessons.title: Talk story, a family interview
lessons.time: Homework plus one class period to share
lessons.text: Students interview a family member, neighbor, or kupuna about a canoe plant in their own life. It could be poi at a baby lūʻau, tī leaves around the house, a noni tree in the yard, or coconut in a family recipe from anywhere in the Pacific or Asia. Students bring back one story and one question they still have. Many of these plants are shared across cultures, so every student has a way in.
questions: Which canoe plants are part of your family's life right now? Did you know their history before this?
What did the person you interviewed know that is not on this website?
How does knowledge about plants get passed down in your family? How is that like or unlike how it was passed down on a voyaging canoe?

lessons.title: Map the journey
lessons.text: Students use The voyage page to trace one plant from its homeland to Hawaiʻi. They mark each stop on a blank Pacific map, estimate the distance of each leg with a map scale, and add dates from the timeline. Then pairs compare a plant from Southeast Asia with ʻuala, which came from the opposite direction.
questions: About how many miles did your plant travel in total? How many generations of people might have carried it?
Why is ʻuala such an important clue about where Polynesian voyagers sailed?
The timeline says older settlement dates for Hawaiʻi were dropped when dating methods improved. Why is it a good thing when scientists change their minds?

lessons.title: Canoe plant or not? A sorting challenge
lessons.text: Write the names of twenty plants on cards. Mix canoe plants with native plants like koa and ʻōhiʻa lehua and later arrivals like mango and pineapple. Crews sort them into three piles. Brought by canoe, already here, and came after 1778. Check the answers with the Myth busters page, then talk about why the wrong guesses felt right.
questions: Which plant surprised you most? Why did you think it was a canoe plant, or think it was not?
What is the difference between a native plant, a canoe plant, and a plant that came after Western contact?
Kou was moved from one pile to another by scientists. What evidence made them do it?

alignment: Nā Hopena Aʻo (HĀ) is the Hawaiʻi Department of Education framework of six outcomes. Belonging, Responsibility, Excellence, Aloha, Total well being, and Hawaiʻi. This site connects most directly to a strengthened sense of Hawaiʻi and of Belonging, because students learn the plants, places, and stories of the islands they live on. The garden and interview lessons build Responsibility and Aloha through caring for living things and listening to elders.

In science, the site supports work on ecosystems, on how living things are suited to where they grow, and on how people change the places they settle. The arrival of people, plants, and animals in Hawaiʻi is a clear local case study of human impact on an island ecosystem. The voyage page also models how scientists use evidence from different fields and revise their ideas.

In social studies, it supports units on Polynesian migration, early Hawaiian society, and the ahupuaʻa system. We have not listed specific standard codes. Please match the lessons to your own grade level standards.
pronunciation: Hawaiian has five vowels. A sounds like ah, e like the e in bet, i like ee in see, o like oh, and u like oo in moon.
The ʻokina (ʻ) is a consonant. It is a quick stop in the throat, like the break in the middle of uh-oh. Maiʻa has three beats. Mai, stop, a.
The kahakō is the line over a vowel, as in kō or kī. Hold that vowel a little longer. It can change the meaning of a word completely, so it is never optional.
The stress usually falls on the second to last syllable, or on a vowel with a kahakō.
Every plant page has a simple sound guide under the name. When in doubt, ask a Hawaiian language speaker at your school. It is always fine to ask.
